 The Board of Supervisors heard updates from county departments, discussed staffing challenges in General Assistance and reviewed a property tax refund request during its Oct. 27 meeting.
 Potential staffing changes for the county’s General Assistance Department were discussed after Director Kailey Heidemann told supervisors that balancing the department’s growing workload with her Veterans Affairs responsibilities has become increasingly difficult.
 Heidemann said the combination of responsibilities has made it challenging to keep up with client needs, administrative work and communication.
 “I’m not capable enough to split myself into two full-time positions, plus the van ride,” Heidemann told supervisors. “It feels like I have two full-time positions and a part-time position, and I have to try and somehow split that all down into a one full-time period.”
 Heidemann said referrals to General Assistance have increased, along with referrals to other agencies, such as the Veteran’s Affairs Commission. Since July, she estimated receiving approximately 100 emails related to General Assistance.
 Heidemann said she remains concerned about providing adequate service to people who have established working relationships with her.
 “I just feel that I’m not being as helpful as I need to be to those individuals who are needing my help,” she said.
 Supervisors discussed several possible solutions, including hiring a part-time employee, adjusting the division of responsibilities between General Assistance and Veterans Affairs or outsourcing some General Assistance services.
 “We talked about maybe outsourcing general relief to Community Action. You know, they offer that for several counties in the region. So maybe we’ll go back and look at the costs associated with that and compare it to segregation of duties,” Supervisor Corey Cerwinske suggested revisiting the possibility of contracting with Community Action, which provides general relief services for several counties in the region.
 He also said the board would need to evaluate the costs and responsibilities associated with that option.
 Supervisor Bob Brunkhorst said the board would need to work with the appropriate commission to determine how Heidemann’s time should be divided.
 Heidemann emphasized that a change is necessary to ensure the departments and their clients receive adequate attention.
 Roadside Vegetation Management Sees Increased Efficiency 
 Roadside Vegetation Management Director Nick Joss reported improvements in the county’s weed control efforts following the first full year of using a new spray system.
 Joss said the system has allowed the department to cover significantly more ground while reducing the amount of time spent stopping to complete paperwork.
 In 2024, the department recorded approximately 720 miles driven while spraying. This year, that figure increased to just under 2,300 miles.
 The system allows workers to identify and spot-spray individual weeds rather than continuously spraying roadside areas. Joss estimated that of the approximately 15 miles driven each day, about 1 mile involved actual spraying.
 “We can cover more; we don’t have to stop as much,” Joss said.
 The system also electronically records spraying information, which can be uploaded to a computer and used to generate reports for the Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship.
 Joss noted that the department used more herbicides this year because of the increased coverage. However, rising costs have prompted him to explore ways to reduce expenses, such as applying for a grant to upgrade the sprayer with larger tanks that would allow the department to purchase herbicide in bulk and automatically regulate the dosage.
 Currently, the department purchases 15-gallon barrels of herbicide. A pallet of nine barrels costs nearly $10,000, Joss said, with prices expected to increase.
 Joss also reported improvements in controlling several noxious weeds, including musk thistle and Japanese knotweed. Japanese knotweed was added to the state’s noxious weed list in July, and the department is continuing to monitor and control it.
 He encouraged property owners to help manage noxious weeds on private property, noting that the county would prefer voluntary cooperation over enforcement.
 Joss said he has been sharing information and photographs through the department’s Facebook page to help residents identify problem plants. He also offered to help landowners develop management plans.
 Joss also plans to establish a roadside vegetation demonstration plot near Frederika. The project will involve preparing an area over the winter, followed by burning, herbicide application and spring planting.
 Educational signs will be placed at the site to help residents understand the process and the purpose of the project.
 Growmark Property Tax Refund Request 
 The board discussed a property tax refund request from Growmark Inc. involving above-ground storage tanks.
 The request stems from a recent Iowa Supreme Court decision concerning the taxation of certain storage tanks. Similar refund requests are being considered by counties across the state.
 Growmark, an agricultural cooperative that provides grain marketing products and services, is seeking a refund of taxes paid for the 2023 assessment year under Iowa Code 445.60.
 Robinson said supervisors will need to determine whether the original assessment involved an irregular tax or an illegal tax under the Supreme Court’s ruling. The distinction affects whether Growmark was required to exhaust administrative appeal options before requesting a refund.
 He also noted that supervisors will need to determine whether the company’s request was filed within the required time frame.
 The county has already adjusted the assessments for 2024, 2025 and 2026 following the court decision, according to county staff.
 Robinson recommended bringing Growmark representatives before the board to present their position and allow supervisors to review the circumstances before making a decision.
 Supervisors agreed to schedule the matter for discussion Nov. 17.
 The board also accepted and placed on file Treasurer Adam Hoffman’s semiannual report covering the final six months of fiscal year 2026.
